pages.name: Birmingham
pages.blurb: Network Records named the genre; Downwards and House of God hardened it; the Que Club housed it.

pages.name: Cologne
pages.blurb: Kompakt, and WDR's electronic studio before it.

pages.name: Düsseldorf
pages.blurb: Kraftwerk's Kling Klang studio.

pages.name: Frankfurt
pages.blurb: Trance's birthplace, and schranz's: Dorian Gray, Omen, Sven Väth, Harthouse.

pages.name: London
pages.blurb: Camden Palace and Clink Street, Shoom and Spectrum, the M25 raves, pirate radio, Lost, The End, Stay Up Forever, fabric, Fold.

pages.name: Milton Keynes
pages.blurb: The Sanctuary, hardcore's home, with Helter Skelter and Dreamscape.

pages.name: Paris
pages.blurb: Rex Club, Laurent Garnier, F Communications, the teknivals.

pages.name: Shinjuku Ni-chōme
pages.blurb: Tokyo's gay district, with more than 300 venues in five blocks according to a 2026 guide.

pages.name: Tbilisi
pages.blurb: Bassiani and Khidi; the 2018 raid and the dancing protest.

pages.name: Above the Stag Theatre, Vauxhall
queries: "Above the Stag Theatre, Vauxhall" London nightclub
pages.blurb: LGBTQ+ theatre in a Vauxhall railway arch that announced on 7 August 2022 that it had closed, citing its finances and Network Rail safety work.

pages.name: Area, Vauxhall
pages.blurb: Larger club beside Crash in the Vauxhall arches, opened by Wayne Shires.

pages.name: Bagley's
pages.blurb: King's Cross warehouses: Slammin' Vinyl and the licensed rave's London home; renamed Canvas in 2003, closed January 2008.

pages.name: Berghain / Panorama Bar
pages.blurb: A 1953 power plant, with Panorama Bar from October 2004 and the main floor from December; Funktion-One and Klubnacht.

pages.name: Brilliant Corners
pages.blurb: Dalston bar run by Amit and Aneesh Patel, playing jazz, disco and electronic records through Klipschorns.

pages.name: Cairo Jazz Club
pages.blurb: Mohandiseen live-music club opened in 2001 by three musician and artist partners, with no cover charge.

pages.name: RIP at Clink Street
pages.blurb: Paul Stone and Lu Vukovic's Friday-and-Saturday parties in a Southwark warehouse beside the old Clink prison: Mr. C and Eddie Richards resident, Kid Batchelor; the dark twin of Shoom, and where London heard Detroit. "Revolution in Progress".

pages.name: Corsica Studios
pages.blurb: Two rooms under the railway arches at Elephant and Castle; the small club that booked everything first. In 2026 it announced it would close in its current form.

pages.name: D-Edge
pages.blurb: Club founded by Renato Ratier in Campo Grande in 2000, opened in Barra Funda, São Paulo, on 28 April 2003.

pages.name: Dorian Gray
pages.blurb: In the airport; Väth's first residency; open until Monday.

pages.name: The Eagle, Vauxhall
pages.blurb: Kennington Lane pub-club, called Dukes when Horse Meat Disco arrived on New Year's Day 2004; from 2022 also home to Duckie by day.

pages.name: fabric
pages.blurb: Three rooms under Smithfield; the bodysonic floor; closed September 2016, reopened January 2017.

pages.name: Flying
pages.blurb: Started at Queens in Slough in 1989 by Brandon Block and Dean Thatcher, promoted and later run by Charlie Chester; Italian house in 1990–91.

pages.name: G-Mex
pages.blurb: The Manchester hall where 808 State opened for Happy Mondays in March 1990 and headlined the In Your Face Turbo Rave a year later.

pages.name: Gold
pages.blurb: Tokyo's bubble-era mega club in a converted seven-storey warehouse on the Shibaura canal; Larry Levan and François K played its Harmony Tour.

pages.name: The Haçienda
pages.blurb: FAC 51; empty for years, then Nude (1986) and Hot (1988) made it Britain's first house club; closed by guns and debt.

pages.name: Hï Ibiza
pages.blurb: The Night League's club in Space's old Platja d'en Bossa building, opened May 2017; voted world number one by DJ Mag readers from 2022 to 2025.

pages.name: I-Beam
pages.blurb: Gay disco and later rock venue at 1748 Haight Street, with Michael Garrett as main DJ from 1980 to 1992; closed after neighbour noise complaints.

pages.name: Kabareet
pages.blurb: Palestinian-run Haifa club, home to Jazar Crew's parties, which closed for good in September 2024.

pages.name: Klub K4
pages.blurb: Basement club at Kersnikova 4, formally established in 1989, an early Ljubljana techno venue, where Umek and Valentino Kanzyani started.

pages.name: Labyrinth Club
pages.blurb: Hasselt club where Amelie Lens won a residency in 2013 and curated the Exhale nights.

pages.name: Le Pulp
pages.blurb: Small lesbian-run club on the Grands Boulevards with free entry, residencies for Chloé and Jennifer Cardini, and the Kill the DJ party.

pages.name: Metropol (Berlin)
pages.blurb: Studio 54-inspired Schöneberg disco on Nollendorfplatz that turned increasingly gay from around 1980 and gave Westbam a residency.

pages.name: The Music Box
pages.blurb: Ron Hardy's club; the first floor for Acid Tracks.

pages.name: Nine Bar
pages.blurb: Clifftop bar at Ozran above Little Vagator that began as a tea shack; its sunset-to-10pm trance sessions drew 1,000-plus in the 1990s.

pages.name: Otel'
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: Club in the ribbon factory's old boiler house, opened April 2014; where Cxema's first party was held, by the Kyiv Post's and Don't Take Fake's accounts; a volunteer base and shelter in 2022.

pages.name: Paradise Factory
pages.blurb: Peter Dalton's Princess Street house club, a little apart from Canal Street, remembered in reunion parties until 2014.

pages.name: Pikes
pages.blurb: Tony Pike's farmhouse hotel outside Sant Antoni, opened 1980: Wham!'s pool, Freddie Mercury's party, and since the Ibiza Rocks takeover a DJs' retreat.

pages.name: Printworks
pages.blurb: The Press Halls in Canada Water.

pages.name: Rage at Heaven
pages.blurb: Fabio and Grooverider's Thursday: Belgian techno, then breaks at 45 rpm, then jungle.

pages.name: Royal Vauxhall Tavern
pages.blurb: Vauxhall pub and queer venue, Grade II listed on 8 September 2015 after the RVT Future campaign.

pages.name: The Shelter
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: Club in a former bomb shelter on Yongfu Road, co-founded by Gareth (Gaz) Williams and Gary Wang; Resident Advisor reported in October 2016 that its licence could not be renewed, and its last party was on New Year's Eve 2016.

pages.name: Space
pages.blurb: Playa d'en Bossa, the Terrace under the flight path; Carl Cox 2001–16; ENTER.; closed 2 October 2016.

pages.name: Studio 54
pages.blurb: Steve Rubell and Ian Schrager's club in a former CBS studio at 254 West 54th Street, with a Richard Long system.

pages.name: The EndUp
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: Former hotel at Sixth and Harrison where the Sunday tea dance and 6 am Church party fed a weekend that ran close to 50 hours.

pages.name: The Outcast
pages.blurb: Motorcycle club that held about 2,500 people from 2 a.m. to 7 a.m. and was the main room of Detroit's ghettotech years.

pages.name: The Stud (San Francisco)
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: South of Market dance bar, collectively owned from 2016, that closed in 2020 and reopened at 1123 Folsom Street in 2024.

pages.name: Trocadero Transfer
pages.blurb: Dick Collier's club at 520 Fourth Street with a Graebar system, where Bobby Viteritti played from 1977 to 1981.

pages.name: UNVRS
pages.blurb: The Night League's 'hyperclub' on the old Ku and Privilege site near Sant Rafel, opened May 2025 with a different residency every night of the week.

pages.name: The Warehouse
pages.blurb: Frankie Knuckles's club; the music was named after it.

pages.name: Womb
pages.blurb: Shibuya; the mirrorball the size of a car.

pages.name: Zouk
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: Lincoln Cheng's club in three 1919 warehouses on Jiak Kim Street from 1991; Genting Hong Kong took over in 2015; Clarke Quay from 2016.

pages.name: BBC Radiophonic Workshop
pages.blurb: The BBC's electronic sound unit at Maida Vale, opened in 1958 with Daphne Oram as its first studio manager.

pages.name: Brick Bandits
pages.blurb: Newark crew founded by Tim Dolla and Mike V, later joined by DJ Tameil, with chapters in Philadelphia and Chicago.

pages.name: Cxema
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: Slava Lepsheev's rave series, begun April 2014, held in skateparks, garages and film-studio pavilions; holding daytime parties by March 2026, CNN reported.

pages.name: Dreem Teem
pages.blurb: DJ Spoony, Mikee B and Timmi Magic, who met on the pirate London Underground, took garage to Kiss and Galaxy FM and joined BBC Radio 1 in January 2000.

pages.name: Future Terror
pages.blurb: DJ Nobu's techno and house party, started in Chiba in 2001 to book his friends and later moved to Tokyo; Haruka joined later.

pages.name: Horse Meat Disco
pages.blurb: Disco party begun on New Year's Day 2004 at Dukes in Vauxhall by Hillard, Howard, Stanton and Panzetta; four Strut compilations.

pages.name: Keychange
pages.blurb: PRS Foundation scheme launched in 2017 with a 50:50 line-up pledge for 2022; later run from Reeperbahn Festival and Brussels.

pages.name: Magnetic Man
pages.blurb: Skream, Benga and Artwork's live trio, whose 2010 album on Columbia reached number five in Britain.

pages.name: MFR Souls
pages.blurb: Katlehong duo of Maero and Force Reloaded who say they pioneered amapiano; 'Amanikiniki' set off a nationwide TikTok dance craze in 2020.

pages.name: Orange (Orange Nation)
pages.blurb: Sunday night that began at Fire in Vauxhall in 2003 and gave its name to the promoter behind the club's long weekend.

pages.name: Q-dance
pages.blurb: Dutch hardstyle promoter co-founded by Wouter Tavecchio and by 2024 part of ID&T; ran Qlimax until 2024, and Defqon.1.

pages.name: Rudeboyz
pages.blurb: KwaMashu gqom group whose 2015 EP on Goon Club Allstars was many listeners' first taste of the sound.

pages.name: SISTER
pages.blurb: Network of women and gender non-conforming electronic music professionals, grown from a Facebook group begun by TOXE and led by Lenora Thornton.

pages.name: Sugarlump
pages.blurb: London sound system that ran an acid house marquee behind a Glastonbury market stall in 1989 and a 24-hour rig in 1992.

pages.name: TOPLAP
pages.blurb: Live-coding organisation formed in a Hamburg bar; its manifesto asks performers to show their screens.

pages.name: Your Sisters' House
pages.blurb: Women-led Thursday rave benefit founded by Liz Roberts in 1993, combining a dinner, a forum and a dance.

pages.name: AfrikaBurn
pages.blurb: Burning Man's South African offshoot in the Tankwa Karoo, from about 1,000 people in 2007 to 10,728 ticket holders in 2025, by its own counts.

pages.name: Apocalypse Now
pages.blurb: Tony Colston-Hayter's 1988 studio parties in London, sold as private events and filmed by TV news; the commercial model that became Sunrise.

pages.name: Asylum and Pyramid at Heaven
queries: "Asylum and Pyramid at Heaven" London nightclub
pages.blurb: Kevin Millins's Thursday at Heaven from 14 April 1983 with Colin Faver and Mark Moore; by 1985 it had become Pyramid, which the Museum of London counts among the first clubs in the country to play Chicago house.

pages.name: Awakenings
pages.blurb: 30 March 1997, the Gashouder; Spaarnwoude.

pages.name: Balad Beast
pages.blurb: MDLBeast's festival in Al-Balad, Jeddah's old town and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, first held in December 2022 with a 12,000 daily cap.

pages.name: Bedrock (club night)
pages.blurb: John Digweed and Nick Muir's Bedrock as a night: monthly at Heaven in London and at The Beach in Brighton from 2000 to 2005.

pages.name: Biology
pages.blurb: London promotion of Jarvis Sandy and Tarquin de Meza: in 1989 it staged the rave as a concert, with stage, sound and lasers in a field.

pages.name: Bloc
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: Alex Benson and George Hull's holiday-camp electronic weekender; collapsed at the London Pleasure Gardens in July 2012.

pages.name: The BPM Festival
pages.blurb: Ten-day January festival in Playa del Carmen until the shooting of 16 January 2017; announced a September 2017 edition at Praia da Rocha, Portimão.

pages.name: Burning Man
pages.blurb: Week-long participant-built city in Nevada's Black Rock Desert, begun on Baker Beach in 1986; 78,850 people in 2019.

pages.name: Club Dog
pages.blurb: Weekly Friday of psychedelic bands, films and light shows in Wood Green and then at the Sir George Robey, Finsbury Park; the root of Megadog.

pages.name: Creamfields
pages.blurb: Cream's festival; the superclub outdoors.

pages.name: Dance Valley
pages.blurb: Daytime dance festival at Spaarnwoude near Velsen since 1995; its 2001 edition for 90,000 ended in rain and hypothermia.

pages.name: DJ Mag Top 100 DJs 2025
pages.blurb: Announced at UNVRS Ibiza on 30 September 2025; Charlotte de Witte placed ninth, her first top-ten place.

pages.name: Detroit Techno Militia in Hastings
queries: "Detroit Techno Militia in Hastings" "The Pig, Hastings"
"Detroit Techno Militia in Hastings" Hastings nightclub
pages.blurb: Easter Sunday 2023 (the first), 27 December 2024 at The Pig, Easter Sunday 5 April 2026 at the Deep End, Brewing Brothers Courtyard: T.Linder, DJ Seoul and J.Garcia from the 313, with DJK, Japhy and Rob Miller.

pages.name: Earthcore
pages.blurb: Spiro Boursine's Victorian bush doof, begun at Toolangi in 1993, on hiatus until 2013 and last held in 2017.

pages.name: Electric Picnic
pages.blurb: John Reynolds's festival at Stradbally Hall, County Laois; Festival Republic bought 71 per cent in 2009.

pages.name: Escape from Samsara
pages.blurb: Hard trance night at the Fridge in Brixton, started by Tim Samsara and a partner, Richard: monthly from September 1995, every Friday from May 1997 to 2002, with reunions from 2006.

pages.name: Fantazia
pages.blurb: Promoters from Cheltenham: stately homes, Westpoint, 25,000; then videos, albums and merchandise.

pages.name: Flower Power
pages.blurb: Pacha's 1960s night, started in 1980 or 1981 and still running, with Piti Urgell; the Guardian calls it the club's earliest themed party.

pages.name: Fruit Machine
pages.blurb: Heaven's Wednesday night in the 1990s, hosted by Miss Kimberley.

pages.name: FWD>>
pages.blurb: The night begun at the Velvet Rooms in Soho in 2001 by Sarah Lockhart and Ammunition, later at Plastic People in Shoreditch.

pages.name: Glastonbury Dance Tent / Dance Village / Silver Hayes
queries: "Glastonbury Dance Tent / Dance Village / Silver Hayes"
pages.blurb: Glastonbury's dance area: a single tent from 1995, the eight-venue Dance Village from 2005 and Silver Hayes from 2013.

pages.name: Goa full-moon parties
pages.blurb: Dusk-to-dawn parties on north Goa's beaches and in its woods, timed to the full moon and Christmas–New Year: bands in the 1970s, DJs from the 1980s.

pages.name: Home of La Troya
pages.blurb: Brasilio de Oliveira's gay night, from Privilege and Amnesia to Wednesdays at Space.

pages.name: Hot at the Haçienda
pages.blurb: Mike Pickering and Jon Dasilva's Wednesday at the Haçienda from July 1988, opened with palm trees, beach balls and a 20-foot swimming pool, replacing Paul Cons's Zumbar.

pages.name: Jive Turkey
pages.blurb: Winston Hazel and Parrot's Friday night in Sheffield, listed with Occasions as the city's soul-into-bleep nights of 1985 to 1990.

pages.name: Kappa FuturFestival
pages.blurb: Turin's July daytime festival at Parco Dora, a park on a former Michelin site; 125,000 people reported in 2026.

pages.name: The Konstantin interview row
pages.blurb: June 2017 Groove interview remarks by Giegling's Konstantin led to Sunfall cancelling a Giegling session and a 2018 ADE petition.

pages.name: Lightning in a Bottle
pages.blurb: Do LaB's California festival, grown from a birthday party for Jesse Flemming's friends into a five-day event.

pages.name: Love Muscle
pages.blurb: The Fridge's Saturday from September 1992: uplifting house, go-go dancers and stage shows, with Yvette the Conqueror as hostess; it ended at the Fridge in 2004 and was later revived.

pages.name: Magnetic Fields
pages.blurb: Wild City's festival at Alsisar Mahal, a palace in Rajasthan's Shekhawati region, from 2013; succeeded in 2026 by Nomads at Khetri.

pages.name: Megatripolis
pages.blurb: Fraser Clark's Thursday club at Heaven: trance and ambient rooms, market stalls and a talk room where McKenna, Ginsberg and Leary appeared.

pages.name: Moga Festival
pages.blurb: Matthieu Corosine's festival begun in Essaouira in 2016; its main edition moved to Caparica, near Lisbon, after the pandemic.

pages.name: Music Is Revolution
pages.blurb: Carl Cox's Tuesday residency at Space, sixteen summers from 2001; its 2016 season was The Final Chapter and the last night was 20 September 2016.

pages.name: Nature One
pages.blurb: A rocket base in the Hunsrück.

pages.name: Notting Hill Carnival
pages.blurb: West London's August street carnival; sound systems invited in 1973, now more than 30 static systems.

pages.name: Parada Wolności
pages.blurb: Łódź's Freedom Parade, run by the New Alcatraz crew; about 80,000 took part in 2002, RMF24 reported, before a new mayor banned it, as DJ Mag tells it.

pages.name: Pendragon
pages.blurb: Trance crew whose usual base was the Theatre Factory, a warehouse on Tyssen Street in Dalston; it sometimes took the Fridge's fifth Friday and helped with Escape from Samsara's décor.

pages.name: Qlimax
pages.blurb: Q-dance's indoor hardstyle show at the GelreDome in Arnhem; the last, "The Final Prophecy", was held on 16 November 2024.

pages.name: Reclaim the Streets
pages.blurb: Sound systems and road protest, with the party as occupation.

pages.name: Sabresonic
pages.blurb: Andrew Weatherall's Friday techno night at Happy Jax under London Bridge, where the Chemical Brothers played their first live gig.

pages.name: Secret Garden Party
pages.blurb: Freddie Fellowes's Cambridgeshire party, where The Loop opened public drug checking in 2016; returned in 2022.

pages.name: Shambala Festival
pages.blurb: Independent, sponsor-free Northamptonshire festival, meat and fish free since 2016; in April 2026 it announced a move to employee ownership.

pages.name: Sleaze Ball
pages.blurb: Mardi Gras fundraiser launched in 1982 at Paddington Town Hall, a Hi-NRG and disco all-nighter that later moved to the Hordern Pavilion.

pages.name: Soundstorm
pages.blurb: MDLBeast's festival at Banban, north of Riyadh, first held as MDL Beast on 19–21 December 2019; the 2026 edition was called off.

pages.name: Strichka
pages.blurb: Closer's spring festival, begun around Nastia's birthday party in 2014; it came to run for more than 30 hours across seven floors of the ribbon factory.

pages.name: Sunburn
pages.blurb: Percept's EDM festival, first held on Candolim beach in December 2007; Vagator from 2013, Pune 2016–18, Goa again 2019–24, Mumbai in 2025.

pages.name: The teknival
pages.blurb: Free festivals across France and Europe, born of Spiral Tribe's exile.

pages.name: The Mother
pages.blurb: Planned free festival stopped by police across several counties; Black Moon's rig was seized and three crew prosecuted under section 63.

pages.name: Tomorrowland Brasil
pages.blurb: Tomorrowland's Brazilian edition at Parque Maeda, Itu: 180,000 tickets in 2015; a storm cancelled its Friday in 2023.

pages.name: Tribal Gathering / Universe
pages.blurb: Universe's licensed answer to the CJA: 25,000 at Lower Pertwood in 1993; Kraftwerk in 1997.

pages.name: Ultra Korea
pages.blurb: The first Ultra event in Asia, opened in Seoul in 2012.

pages.name: Untold
pages.blurb: Cluj-Napoca's August festival, opened at Cluj Arena in 2015; Romania Insider reported more than 470,000 people in 2025.

pages.name: WetYourSelf!
pages.blurb: Sunday night of underground house and techno at fabric from February 2009, with Peter Pixzel, Jacob Husley, Carlos Ryan and Lamine.

pages.name: Wire
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: Takkyu Ishino's all-night indoor techno rave, at Yokohama Arena except for two years at Saitama Super Arena (2002–03), inspired by Germany's Mayday; Wire13 in 2013 was the last to date.

pages.name: XP Music Futures
pages.blurb: MDLBeast's music-industry conference, first held at Jax in Riyadh on 13–15 December 2021, the three days before Soundstorm.

pages.name: Berlin's club noise protection fund
pages.blurb: €1 million pledged in December 2017 for soundproofing clubs, outdoor barriers and neighbours' windows.

pages.name: The fabric closure, 2016
pages.blurb: Islington revoked fabric's licence after two deaths; the campaign, a crowdfund of over £330,000 and the reopening in January 2017 under new conditions.

pages.name: MDMA
pages.blurb: Synthesised by Merck in 1912, used in therapy in the 1970s, banned in the US in 1985 and Britain in 1977; the drug the music is inseparable from.

pages.name: Noise Council Code of Practice on Environmental Noise Control at Concerts
queries: "Noise Council Code of Practice on Environmental Noise Control at Concerts" London
"Noise Council Code of Practice on Environmental Noise Control at Concerts"
pages.blurb: The 'Pop Code': 65 or 75 dB(A) over 15 minutes at 1 m from a façade; inaudible indoors after 11pm.

pages.name: The Loop
pages.blurb: Fiona Measham's drug-checking charity, which ran the first front-of-house testing at a UK festival, Secret Garden Party 2016.

pages.name: Akai S1000
pages.blurb: Sampler — Stereo, CD-quality, and a timestretch that could slow a vocal without lowering it: the smear that became jungle's signature. ("Terminator" itself was pitch-shifted through an Eventide H3000, by 4hero's account; the S1000 put the stretching trick in every bedroom.)

pages.name: AlphaTheta Euphonia
pages.blurb: Four-channel rotary mixer with Rupert Neve Designs transformer circuit; the first AlphaTheta-branded product, March 2024, $3,799 / £3,249.

pages.name: Novation Bass Station
pages.blurb: Monosynth — Novation's first synth (1993): a cheap analogue bass box with a Wasp filter, sold as a way round the scarce TB-303 and a fixture of 1990s acid.

pages.name: Pioneer CDJ-1000
pages.blurb: CD deck — Pioneer's 2001 deck with a turntable-sized platter and Vinyl Mode became the booth standard; USB came in 2007, the networked CDJ-2000 in 2009.

pages.name: AlphaTheta CDJ-3000X
pages.blurb: AlphaTheta-branded successor of September 2025: 10.1-inch screen, Wi-Fi, Beatport and TIDAL streaming, USB-C, no SD slot.

pages.name: Commodore Amiga
pages.blurb: Home computer whose Paula chip played four channels of 8-bit sound and made the tracker, and much early hardcore, possible.

pages.name: Argon and krypton display lasers
pages.blurb: Water-cooled ion lasers of up to tens of watts, run by specialist crews and split through fibre heads at the big licensed raves.

pages.name: Elektron Machinedrum / Octatrack
pages.blurb: Hardware groovebox — Elektron's Machinedrum (2001) and Octatrack (2011): Swedish sequencer-led boxes at the heart of the 2010s hardware live set.

pages.name: The Festival System
pages.blurb: Tony Andrews's pre-Turbosound festival PA: double-18 folded-horn bins, twin 10-inch Turbo mids and horn-loaded highs in separate cabinets.

pages.name: GarageBand
pages.blurb: Apple's entry-level studio, announced by Steve Jobs on 6 January 2004 and developed under Gerhard Lengeling.

pages.name: Roland Juno-60 / Juno-106
pages.blurb: Polysynth — The warm, cheap polysynth with the chorus button, behind the pads of deep house and, per Roland, the bassline of "Can You Feel It".

pages.name: L-Acoustics V-DOSC
pages.blurb: Line-source array developed in 1992 from Heil's Wavefront Sculpture theory, coupling a column of boxes into one wavefront.

pages.name: Native Instruments Massive
pages.blurb: Mike Daliot's wavetable bass synth, slow to sell at first; by Native Instruments' own account its success came in dubstep.

pages.name: PLAYdifferently Model 1
pages.blurb: DJ mixer — Hawtin and Andy Rigby-Jones's 2016 analogue mixer: no fixed channel EQ, but Contour filters, a Sculpt band and drive. The Mixer strand borrows it.

pages.name: Native Instruments Stems
pages.blurb: Open four-part audio file format for DJs, announced 30 March 2015 and on sale from 3 August 2015.

pages.name: OctaMED
pages.blurb: Teijo Kinnunen's Amiga tracker, with eight channels and MIDI; Aphrodite, Bizzy B and DJ Zinc are among the producers credited with using it.

pages.name: Pioneer DVJ-X1 / DVJ-1000
pages.blurb: DVD decks that scratched, looped and cued video in sync with sound; the DVJ-1000 was announced at $2,999 in 2006.

pages.name: Rane MP 2016 / XP 2016
pages.blurb: Rane's first rotary mixer and its isolator companion, developed from the Bozak design and numbered by mixing up the UREI's 1620.

pages.name: Propellerhead Reason / ReBirth
pages.blurb: Software — ReBirth (1996) put two 303s and an 808, later a 909, on a screen; Reason (2000) became a patchable rack of virtual hardware.

pages.name: Roland W-30
pages.blurb: Sampling workstation keyboard with a 16-track sequencer on which Liam Howlett made The Prodigy's demo and sequenced their first two albums.

pages.name: Xfer Serum
pages.blurb: Steve Duda's wavetable synth, released September 2014; Serum 2 followed in March 2025 as a free update for owners.

pages.name: E-mu SP-1200
pages.blurb: Sampling drum machine — Ten seconds of 12-bit sampling; hip-hop's machine, and the grit under early hardcore and Todd Terry's house.

pages.name: Stem separation in DJ software
pages.blurb: Machine-learning splitting of finished tracks: djay Pro and VirtualDJ (June 2020), Serato (2022), rekordbox (2023), Traktor Pro 4 (2024).

pages.name: The tape pack
pages.blurb: Boxed sets of up to twelve cassettes of a rave's DJ sets, sold at £15 to £20; Dreamscape issued a five-pack in summer 1993.

pages.name: Technics SL-DZ1200
pages.blurb: Technics's CD and SD-card deck with a ten-inch direct-drive platter, listed at $1,199.95; dropped within about four years.

pages.name: Roland TR-707
pages.blurb: Drum machine — Sampled drums in a plastic box, and the clap and snare of a hundred Chicago jack tracks, Mr. Fingers and Farley among them.

pages.name: Native Instruments Traktor Kontrol S4
pages.blurb: Four-deck Traktor controller with built-in 24-bit sound card and sample decks, announced August 2010 at $999.

pages.name: Ultimate Soundtracker
pages.blurb: Karsten Obarski's Amiga program of 1987, which Xavier Borderie calls the first tracker to use samples, and the origin of the MOD file.

pages.name: Waves L1 Ultramaximizer
pages.blurb: A Pro Tools TDM look-ahead limiter that became a go-to tool of the loudness war.

pages.name: Zero-G Datafile sample CDs
pages.blurb: Ed Stratton's breakbeat and sound CDs, published by Time+Space and sold at £49.95 each in 1992.

pages.name: Progressing Gender Representation in UK Dance Music
queries: "Progressing Gender Representation in UK Dance Music" London
"Progressing Gender Representation in UK Dance Music"
pages.blurb: Jaguar Foundation report of 3 August 2022: 5% of dance chart tracks and under 1% of top radio airplay by women or non-binary artists.

pages.name: Billboard International Disco Sourcebook
pages.blurb: Billboard's annual trade directory, whose polls of discos recorded which turntables, cartridges, mixers and headphones the booths used.

pages.name: The Face
pages.blurb: The style monthly that put acid house on its cover in 1988 and made the smiley a national symbol.

pages.name: Jockey Slut
pages.blurb: Manchester's fanzine turned magazine, the funny, knowledgeable voice of the 1990s underground.

pages.name: NME
pages.blurb: Reported acid house as a moral panic and then as a movement; the 1988 "Summer of Love" coverage.

pages.name: The Purple Guide
pages.blurb: Britain's guide to health, safety and welfare at music events, first published by the HSE (in 1992, by the AIF's account); run by the Events Industry Forum since 2012.

pages.name: Amoeba Music
pages.blurb: Californian record shops founded on Telegraph Avenue, Berkeley, in 1990; San Francisco opened in 1997 and Hollywood in 2001.

pages.name: Buy-Rite Records
pages.blurb: Cliff Thomas's west-side Detroit shop, the city's main source of Chicago house and ghetto-house twelve-inches.

pages.name: Dance Tracks
pages.blurb: East 3rd Street deep-house shop run by Stan Hatzakis, then Joe Claussell and Stefan Prescott; closed 30 November 2007.

pages.name: The Diskery
pages.blurb: Birmingham shop opened by Morris Hunting in 1952; at 99 Bromsgrove Street from 1972, on Bristol Street by 2024. Its imported R&B 45s drew mods.

pages.name: FON Records
pages.blurb: Sheffield's shop and studio before Warp, where the bleep records were sold and some were made.

pages.name: Honest Jon's
pages.blurb: Portobello Road shop begun in a Golborne Road butcher's; James Lavelle and Gilles Peterson worked its counter, and it has run a label since 2002.

pages.name: Kristina Records
pages.blurb: Opened at 44 Stoke Newington Road by Jason Spinks, Jack Rollo and Jamie Thornington; left Dalston in August 2018, reopening on Well Street in 2019.

pages.name: Manchester Underground
pages.blurb: Corn Exchange basement shop opened by three former Spin Inn staff; the 1996 bomb closed its first premises.

pages.name: Piccadilly Records
pages.blurb: Manchester shop that began as a department-store record counter in Piccadilly Plaza and has traded at 53 Oldham Street since 1997.

pages.name: Rhythm Division
pages.blurb: Roman Road shop in Bow tied to the growth of grime, where MCs played dubplates and Wiley filmed a video; a coffee shop replaced it.

pages.name: Rubadub
pages.blurb: Glasgow shop and distributor, begun in Paisley, that imports Detroit, Chicago and New York labels and sells synthesisers at 35 Howard Street.

pages.name: Space Hall
pages.blurb: Kreuzberg shop spread over Zossener Straße 33–35, with house and techno in a dim back room joined to the rest in 2009.

pages.name: Technique
pages.blurb: Shibuya dance-vinyl shop at Udagawacho 33-14, popular with travelling DJs; it moved into Parco in 2020 and shut its doors in March 2022.

pages.name: Vinyl Exchange
pages.blurb: Second-hand shop at 18 Oldham Street, Manchester, whose staff have included Dave Booth and Balearic Mike.

pages.name: Aba Shanti-I
pages.blurb: Dub and roots system that has played Notting Hill Carnival for nearly thirty years, at East Row and Southern Row.

pages.name: Britannia Row Productions
pages.blurb: PA hire company formed by Pink Floyd in 1975 and bought out in 1984; flew 50kW of Turbosound Flashlight at Glastonbury in 1994.

pages.name: d&b audiotechnik
pages.blurb: German loudspeaker maker founded by Jürgen Daubert and Rolf Belz; its Cardioid Subwoofer Array arrived in 2004, the J-Series in 2006.

pages.name: Duke Reid the Trojan
pages.blurb: Former police sergeant Duke Reid's sound, crowned King of Sounds and Blues in the mid-1950s; rival of Coxsone Dodd's Downbeat.

pages.name: Tubby's Hometown Hi-Fi
pages.blurb: King Tubby's own sound, built on his amplifiers, known for echo and reverb and for launching U-Roy; police wrecked it in 1975.

pages.name: Martin Audio
pages.blurb: Dave Martin's London loudspeaker firm of 1971: Pink Floyd's bass bins, the Philishave mid horn and, by 2010–11, award-winning club sound at Ministry of Sound.

pages.name: Richard Long & Associates
pages.blurb: The Paradise Garage system designer: the Levan horns, the bass array, the sound the whole genre was built to be played on.

pages.name: Smokescreen Soundsystem
pages.blurb: Sheffield free-party house system, formed about two years after DiY, that moved to Nottingham in 1997 and kept its parties small after 1994.

pages.name: Turbosound
pages.blurb: Tony Andrews and John Newsham's festival PA firm of 1978: the TMS-3 and Flashlight, sold to Harman in 1992; Funktion-One's predecessor, now a Music Tribe brand.

pages.name: Cercle
pages.blurb: Derek Barbolla's streamed DJ sets, from his Paris flat and then heritage sites, beginning with the Eiffel Tower in 2016; appealed to viewers for support in 2026.

pages.name: Eruption FM
pages.blurb: Waltham Forest's hardcore and jungle pirate on 101.3 FM, on air from February 1993 to February 2012.

pages.name: Lazer FM
pages.blurb: A hardcore pirate of 1990s London, remembered by listeners but barely documented.

pages.name: Top of the Pops
pages.blurb: The BBC chart programme, which made dance acts mime in 1990 and sing live over backing tracks from 3 October 1991.
